strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically relevant vulnerability: the mismatch between training-time load balancing and inference-time routing in MoE models deployed with expert parallelism, and convincingly shows that trivially repetitive prompts concentrate routing on few experts/devices (Figure 4).

The evaluation breadth is a major asset: a survey of 139 HuggingFace MoE configurations, systematic experiments on 14 models spanning low- and high-sparsity designs, multiple EP sizes, and both kernel-level (Rmoe, Table 3) and end-to-end API-level (Rapi, Table 4) latency measurements.

The theoretical TMI analysis (Eq. 3) cleanly characterizes the two regimes (k <= Ed vs. Ed < k) and correctly predicts the deployment dilemma that larger EP amplifies the attack surface; the coverage metric B operationalizes this for empirical measurement.

The paper goes beyond a single attack demo: it shows length/system-prompt robustness (Section 5.1), an interesting analysis of vulnerable-expert distributions across layers (Section 5.2), and proposes two concrete mitigations, including a vulnerability-aware expert placement algorithm evaluated by simulation.
The responsible-disclosure-style ethical statement and defense discussion partially address the inherent dual-use risk of publishing a DoS recipe against commercial APIs.
weaknesses: The DoS impact on other users is asserted but not directly demonstrated. All latency measurements are of the attacker's own requests (Rmoe on the bottleneck GPU, Rapi on its own prompts); there is no experiment showing that co-batched legitimate users actually suffer inflated queuing/TTFT, which is the central 'denial-of-service' claim rather than merely self-latency amplification.

The side-channel claim is under-supported. R_api > 1 on undisclosed APIs (e.g., ChatGPT) is attributed to MoE backends, but the paper does not rule out confounders for highly repetitive inputs: content moderation/filtering pipelines, prefill caching behavior, tokenizer length differences, or provider-specific throttling of degenerate inputs. Notably, the dense control Llama-3-8B-Instruct shows R_api = 1.160 (> 1), which contradicts the stated 'close to or less than 1' characterization; no statistical significance tests are reported despite the text promising a 95% confidence lower bound that never appears in the tables.

Novelty is modest. The core observation (identical tokens route to identical experts) is simple and adjacent to prior work the authors themselves cite (Hayes et al., 2024, buffer overflow in MoE; existing LLM DoS literature). The contribution is more a measurement/systematization of a known fragility than a new technique, and the framing as a universal 'flaw' could be calibrated better against related work.

Mitigation evaluation is simulation-only: the vulnerability-aware load balancing is assessed via the coverage metric B rather than actual vLLM latency measurements, and the PPL-filtering defense is not evaluated for false positives on legitimate repetitive text (code, poetry, logs), nor for its latency overhead beyond a qualitative note.

Reproducibility details are thin: no code or artifact release is mentioned, API provider identification is vague, the number of repetitions/seed control is unclear, and 'we calculate the point estimate' for R_api suggests weak statistical treatment of noisy network measurements.

Several claims are overclaimed or under-evidenced: 'practically optimal' prompt construction is asserted without comparison to searched/optimized baselines (e.g., GCG-style or entropy-maximizing token selection), and the '139 configurations' survey contributes counts of architecture families rather than any vulnerability measurement of those models.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant attack surface: inference-time router imbalance in MoE models under expert parallelism, and links it concretely to TTFT/SLA degradation via a clear systems-level analysis (Amdahl's Law argument, GPU timeline in Figure 2).

The proposed attack (RepetitionCurse) is appealing in its simplicity: it is black-box, requires no gradient access or search, and the paper demonstrates it works across 14 models and reports a broad survey of 139 Hugging Face MoE configurations, which supports the generality claim.

The evaluation includes a layered set of metrics: a theoretical upper bound (TMI), a vocabulary-wide coverage metric B, kernel-level latency amplification (R_moe), and end-to-end API-level amplification (R_api), which together give a reasonably complete picture from routing statistics to real API latency.

The paper goes beyond the attack with analysis (length/system-prompt robustness in Section 5.1, vulnerable-expert heatmaps in Section 5.2) and proposes two concrete mitigations (perplexity filtering and vulnerability-aware expert placement in Algorithm 1), and includes an ethical statement describing responsible testing of commercial APIs.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. Energy-latency ('sponge example') attacks on LLMs via repetitive inputs are well established, and Hayes et al. (2024), cited by the paper itself, already identified MoE routing-related DoS issues. The core attack is essentially 'repeat one token', and the paper does not adequately position or differentiate the contribution against this line of work; the related work section is thin.

Potential confounds in the headline latency results are not ruled out. The comparison is between a single-token-repetition prompt and natural-text prompts; differences in tokenizer behavior, attention kernel performance, and prefix/pattern-dependent engine behaviors could contribute to the observed 3x amplification beyond routing imbalance. The claimed decomposition (attention stable, MoE affected) is asserted but the supporting profiling evidence is not shown in detail.

Statistical rigor is weak for the API measurements. The paper mentions computing a 95% confidence lower bound of R_api, but Table 4 reports only point estimates with no variance, sample-level spread, or significance testing. Given network variability across commercial APIs, the presented evidence is not sufficient to support the precise claims (e.g., the 3.063x figure).

The side-channel claim is over-extended. Inferring that ChatGPT backends are 'likely MoE' from R_api > 1 is speculative: many other factors (safety filtering, repetition handling, different serving stacks, batching policies) could produce latency differences for degenerate repetitive inputs. Two dense-model controls are insufficient to validate the inference, and the paper does not discuss alternative explanations.

The defense evaluation is only a simulation on the routing coverage proxy (bottleneck coverage B), not an end-to-end latency experiment; it is therefore unclear whether the vulnerability-aware placement actually reduces real latency under serving dynamics (batching, EPLB, communication overhead).

Several claims are trivial or overstated. For example, Observation 3 (coverage approaches 1 when EP = E) follows almost by construction, and the abstract's framing that 'nearly all current models are susceptible' is stronger than what the EP-size-dependent coverage curves support, since resistance at common EP settings (16-64) is nontrivial for sparse models.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or artifact release is mentioned, hardware configurations for the local vLLM experiments are unspecified, and details of how network noise was handled for API measurements are insufficient to replicate the results.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely relevant and timely vulnerability: routing imbalance in expert-parallel MoE serving as an algorithmic DoS vector, with a clear and well-scoped threat model (Section 3.1).

The attack (RepetitionCurse) is refreshingly simple and black-box, and the paper does a good job showing why simplicity matters here: no gradient access, no search, robust across prompt lengths (100–16k tokens) and system prompts (Section 5.1).

Broad and systematic empirical grounding: a survey of 139 HuggingFace MoE configurations (Table 1), 14 representative models spanning architectures, sparsity levels, and training stages, plus both simulated router-level analysis (coverage metric B, TMI bound in Eq. 3) and real system-level measurements with vLLM (Table 3) and commercial API measurements (Table 4).

The theoretical TMI analysis (Eq. 3) cleanly characterizes the two regimes (k ≤ Ed vs. Ed < k) and correctly predicts the weaker attack effect on sparse models under EP=8, which the measurements then confirm — good theory–practice alignment.

Goes beyond the headline attack: the side-channel result (inferring MoE backends and coarse EP size from latency ratios, including probing ChatGPT models) and the vulnerable-expert analysis (Section 5.2, early/late-layer vs. intermediate-layer pattern with a plausible 'fallback expert' hypothesis) provide new understanding, not just a new exploit.

Includes concrete defense proposals (PPL filtering, vulnerability-aware expert placement in Algorithm 1) with quantitative evaluation of the placement defense (Figure 8), and an appropriate ethical statement describing responsible testing on commercial APIs.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor of the API-level results is thin. The text claims a '95% confidence lower bound of Rapi' is reported, but Table 4 contains only point estimates. Network jitter, multi-tenancy, and provider-side load balancing are acknowledged as confounds, yet no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests appear in the tables.

The side-channel inference is not airtight. The dense-model controls are ambiguous: Llama-3-8B-Instruct shows Rapi = 1.160 (above 1, contradicting 'close to or less than 1') while Qwen3-14B shows 0.635, suggesting substantial non-routing variance in the measurement. Alternative explanations for Rapi > 1 on commercial APIs (e.g., providers deprioritizing or differently handling highly repetitive 20k-token inputs) are not ruled out, making the 'ChatGPT is likely MoE' conclusion speculative.

The proposed defenses are evaluated only in simulation (coverage metric B after re-planning in Figure 8), not in an actual vLLM deployment, so the real end-to-end effectiveness and overhead of the vulnerability-aware placement defense remain unverified. PPL filtering, moreover, trivially neutralizes the exact prompt form studied; the paper does not test natural evasions (e.g., interleaving varied tokens or padding with natural text) that a motivated attacker would use, leaving the practical severity of the threat somewhat overstated.

Novelty relative to prior work is incremental. Hayes et al. (2024) already identified MoE routing congestion/buffer-overflow issues, and the core observation that OOD inputs concentrate on few experts is closely related to known router-brittle behavior; the main new contributions are the EP-specific straggler analysis, the measurement breadth, and the side-channel.

Practical impact caveats are underexplored: with continuous batching, one adversarial request primarily delays requests co-batched with it rather than the whole cluster; each attack prompt is 20,000 tokens (so cost-per-attack is not negligible despite the 'low-cost' framing); and many providers replicate experts or use dynamic placement (EPLB), which the paper only briefly dismisses as coarse-grained.

No code or artifact release is mentioned, and several experimental details (exact prompt templates, which/how tokens were sampled for the 200 attack prompts, hardware for the system-level experiments) are underspecified, hurting reproducibility.

Presentation issues: the abstract highlights 3.063x on 'Mixtral-8x7B API' as the flagship result, but system-level Rmoe for the same model is only 2.651x at EP=8, and the gap between the two numbers is not fully reconciled; Figure 6's axes and the entropy trend are hard to read; Table 1 mixes architecture percentage with average downloads in a confusing format.

strengths: The paper identifies and rigorously characterizes a genuinely novel attack surface: expert-parallel (EP) deployment as a DoS vector via routing imbalance, which is distinct from prior token-exhaustion DoS attacks (Gao et al., Zhang et al.) in that it degrades compute efficiency per token rather than forcing long generations.

The measurement study is comprehensive and well-organized: a survey of 139 HuggingFace MoE configurations, 13 diverse target models (Mixtral, Qwen3-MoE, GPT-OSS, DeepSeek, Llama-4, Kimi-Linear), EP sizes from 2 to 32, and both local vLLM profiling and black-box commercial API measurements (Table 3).

The attack itself is elegant in its simplicity: a purely black-box, model-agnostic repeated-token prompt with no optimization cost, motivated by a principled formulation (minimizing per-layer embedding variance, Eq. 4) and analyzed against a theoretical upper bound (TMI, Eq. 5) that explains model-dependent behavior.

The paper goes beyond demonstrating the attack: it quantifies SLA degradation with a defensible Log-Normal latency model (Appendix B), evaluates defenses (vulnerability-aware Expert-GPU mapping, EPLB dynamics in Appendix E, PPL filtering in Appendix D), and honestly reports where mitigations work and where they collapse.
Context robustness (Section 6.1) is a valuable addition, showing the vulnerability is invariant to prompt length and system prompts, and that KV-caching does not neutralize it.
A clear impact statement with a stated commitment to responsible disclosure and positioning of the attack as a diagnostic tool.
weaknesses: Research ethics treatment is thin relative to the actions taken. Table 3 reports live measurements against what appear to be commercial third-party LLM APIs (e.g., Kimi, DeepSeek, GPT-OSS endpoints). The paper states only that requests were sent 'at a low request rate with minute-wise intervals' and that 'responsible disclosure' was adopted, but provides no evidence of permission, IRB review, provider notification, timeline, or responses. Deploying latency-degrading requests against production services, even at low rates, likely violates terms of service and needs much stronger ethical justification and documentation.

Novelty relative to Hayes et al. (2024) 'Buffer overflow in Mixture of Experts' needs sharper differentiation. The core phenomenon—repeated tokens causing routing collapse onto a fixed expert subset—appears in that prior work; this paper's contribution is primarily the system-level serving/EP measurement. The paper should more explicitly delineate what is new beyond the deployment context.

The headline '20% to 148%' TTFT increases correspond to the attack-only setting (α = 1); in the more realistic mixed-batch setting (α = 1/2), end-to-end TTFT amplification is only 1.03x–1.65x (Table 2), which is considerably more modest. The abstract and introduction foreground the most favorable numbers without clearly flagging this distinction.

The SLA violation analysis relies on a Log-Normal TTFT distribution assumption and a cited 'P99 TTFT < 20s' chatbot target whose provenance (Gnewuch et al., 2022, a human-chatbot interaction study) is questionable as an SLA benchmark. The claimed jump from P99 to P86.4 depends on the chosen distributional parameters (BurstGPT σ = 0.74 vs. ShareGPT σ = 1.65), and the paper does not measure actual SLA violations under a deployed scheduler.

The attack requires very long prompts (16k–20k tokens); while the paper argues attackers avoid per-token generation costs, attackers still pay full prefill costs for these prompts, partially weakening the 'cheaper DoS' framing. The cost-benefit comparison against baseline DoS attacks (e.g., Crabs) is qualitative rather than quantitative.

No artifact/code release is mentioned, and several experimental details (e.g., batch scheduler configuration, chunked-prefill settings in vLLM, number of seeds/repetitions for latency measurements) are underspecified, which limits reproducibility of the timing results.

The RQ3 'defense' analysis assumes white-box knowledge of trigger-token counts (a vocabulary-wide scan) that a real defender may not cheaply obtain, and the greedy Algorithm 1 is evaluated only in simulation rather than on the actual serving stack.

strengths: The paper identifies and systematically studies a genuine system-level vulnerability: inference-time expert routing imbalance in EP-based MoE serving can be weaponized as a latency-amplification (DoS) vector, a setting distinct from prior token-generation-based DoS attacks.

The measurement is broad: 13 MoE models spanning several architectures (Mixtral-like, Qwen3MoE, GPT-OSS, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Kimi-Linear, Llama-4), multiple EP sizes up to 32 (multi-node for EP=32), plus black-box validation on commercial APIs with confidence-interval reporting.

The framing is well done: the theoretical maximum imbalance (TMI, Eq. 5) analysis cleanly explains the two regimes (k vs E_d) and predicts when bottlenecks saturate, and the RQ1-RQ3 structure (universality, real-world latency/SLA impact, mapping-based mitigation) is coherent.

The paper honestly characterizes limits of its own attack: Section 4.4 discusses obliviousness to expert-GPU mapping and inability to control target experts; RQ3/Appendix C/D/E analyze defenses (vulnerability-aware mapping, EPLB, PPL filtering) rather than strawmanning them.
Robustness checks (prompt length 100-16k, five system prompts, base vs instruction-tuned variants) and the Log-Normal SLA degradation analysis in Appendix B add depth beyond a bare attack demo.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. The core phenomenon (adversarial inputs causing MoE routing concentration) was already identified by Hayes et al. (2024, 'Buffer Overflow in Mixture of Experts'), which the paper cites. The claim of being 'the first to demonstrate that routing imbalance can be weaponized' is not carefully differentiated; the genuine increment is showing that trivial repeated tokens suffice and quantifying system-level TTFT impact, which is more incremental than 'critical vulnerability' framing suggests.

The practical impact at common deployment settings is modest. Under the standard 8-GPU EP setting, TTFT inflation is ~1.1-1.65x (Table 2), and SLA degradation is only P99 -> P98.6 for Qwen3-30B-A3B; the headline 148% / P86.4 numbers require either alpha=1 attack-only flooding or favorable expert-GPU mappings. Additionally, the abstract's '20% to 148%' range is inconsistent with the text's '1.29x to 2.48x'.

Measurement rigor is unclear. Latency results (Table 2) appear to be single runs with no variance or repeat counts reported; batch-composition sensitivity and run-to-run variability of 16k-token prefill batches on A800s are not characterized.

The SLA violation analysis is a projection, not a measurement: it assumes Log-Normal TTFT with scale-invariant sigma under linear latency scaling and O(N) MoE dominance (Appendix B, Figure 9), assumptions that hold only in a specific regime and are not validated end-to-end for the attacked configurations.

Ethics treatment is incomplete. The paper runs attacks against third-party commercial APIs (Table 3: Kimi, DeepSeek-R1-Turbo, GPT-OSS, etc.). While request rates are kept low and responsible disclosure is mentioned, the impact statement does not state whether the operators authorized these experiments, which is a material requirement for such work.
Reproducibility is not addressed: no code/artifact release is mentioned, and key attack details (which leading token is modified to bypass KV caching, exact prompt templates) are underspecified.

Some claims are under-supported or internally inconsistent: the intro asserts the vulnerability is 'primarily introduced during pretraining' from a single observation about same-family models; the embedding-variance motivation (Eqs. 3-4) is heuristic and never empirically connected to Eq. 5's TMI or measured bottleneck; Figure 6/7 presentation is hard to parse.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed threat: the paper convincingly identifies a system-level gap between training-time balancing losses and inference-time expert parallelism deployment, turning MoE efficiency mechanisms into a DoS vector against TTFT/SLA. The framing as 'turning parallelism against itself' is compelling.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 13 models spanning Mixtral-like, DeepSeek/Qwen sparse, GPT-OSS, and linear-attention architectures, EP sizes from 2 to 32 on real 8x A800 hardware (multi-node for larger EP), plus a survey of 139 HuggingFace MoE configurations to establish representativeness.

Both attack-side and defense-side analysis: the paper derives a theoretical upper bound on imbalance (TMI, Eq. 5), explains practical constraints (expert-GPU mapping obliviousness, inability to control targets), and evaluates mitigations including vulnerability-aware mapping (Alg. 1) and dynamic EPLB (Appendix E), honestly showing defenses are only partial.

Strong ecological validity: end-to-end evaluation on commercial APIs (Table 3) with 95% CI lower bounds, and an SLA violation analysis (Appendix B) grounded in Log-Normal fits to real BurstGPT/ShareGPT workload distributions.

Robustness and generality checks: results hold across prompt lengths (100-16k), diverse system prompts, base vs. instruction-tuned variants, and nearly the entire vocabulary (bottleneck coverage approaching 1 at EP=E), supporting the claim that this is an intrinsic architectural issue rather than a tuned attack.
Responsible presentation: attack rate was kept low against commercial APIs, an impact statement is included, and the attack is positioned as a diagnostic tool.
weaknesses: Novelty of the core observation is overstated. The claim of being 'the first to demonstrate that routing imbalance can be weaponized' sits uneasily with prior work: Hayes et al. (2024) already studied MoE routing/buffer manipulation via repeated tokens, and He et al. (2025) explicitly studies the straggler effect in MoE inference. The paper cites both but does not clearly delineate what is new beyond scaling the measurement and the SLA/DoS framing.

The attack is extremely simple (repeated tokens), which is a strength for practicality but weakens technical depth; the connection between the objective in Eq. (4) and the repeated-token heuristic is asserted empirically rather than formally, and no stronger gradient-free baseline (e.g., token search) is compared against.

Key results depend on default static expert-GPU mapping and single-batch settings (16,384-token batches, fixed alpha). Real deployments with EPLB enabled degrade the effect substantially (Table 7 shows reductions, e.g., Mixtral B dropping from 0.56 to 0.52-0.54; Qwen3 at EP=32 from 0.38 to 0.33), and the claimed LARs (1.29x-2.48x TTFT at EP=8 for Mixtral) shrink to ~1.2x-2.2x or less for sparser models at common EP settings. The practical severity for well-configured production systems is therefore more modest than the abstract suggests.

The defense discussion dismisses perplexity-based filtering somewhat quickly: while the PPL analysis (Table 6) is useful, a trivially deployable filter (length-normalized repetition ratio, n-gram entropy, or a lightweight classifier) is neither proposed nor evaluated; the paper argues only against one specific defense instantiation. A stronger treatment of practical defenses would materially improve the contribution.

The SLA degradation analysis assumes TTFT scales linearly with MoE latency (sigma invariance under linear scaling), which is justified by profiling one model (Qwen3-30B-A3B, Fig. 9) but is not validated for the other architectures to which it is extrapolated.

API experiments are thin: 100 prompts per API at 20,000 tokens each, single run, no measurement of effect on co-batched benign users or sustained load; LARapi conflates network variance with server-side routing effects despite the CILB treatment. The attacker cost of submitting 20k-token prompts is also not analyzed against the induced damage.

Reproducibility: no artifact/code release is mentioned; given that results hinge on specific vLLM versions, profiling configurations, and exact prompt constructions, a reproducibility statement would be needed.

Minor: some metrics (bottleneck coverage B, Eq. 6) mix device-level normalization with per-layer maxima in ways that are hard to interpret intuitively, and Figure 7/8 annotation placement could be clearer.
